{"summary":"Architecture memo — recommend a macOS 26 LSUIElement app with an AppKit menu-bar shell (`NSStatusItem` plus transient `NSPopover`) hosting a dense SwiftUI dashboard. The popover presents exactly three fixed workspaces: dev, playgrounds, and personal. Keep the existing MSW 3.1.0 CLI as the sole lifecycle authority; the app is a typed, asynchronous front end, not a second MicroSandbox implementation.

Menu-bar choice: `MenuBarExtra` with `.window` is available from macOS 13 and is excellent for a small, mostly declarative utility. Apple describes it as a popover-like window for complex or data-rich content. Its public insertion binding controls whether the status item exists, not whether its window is currently presented, and a menu-bar-only app can be terminated if the user removes the extra. `NSStatusItem`/`NSPopover` adds some AppKit glue but provides explicit show, close, anchoring, transient behavior, event handling, status-item persistence, and reliable keyboard/focus control. Those controls matter for long-running VM operations, error presentation, and reopening the panel, so AppKit is the shippable choice. Keep the popover content entirely in SwiftUI through `NSHostingController`. `MenuBarExtra` and its window style require macOS 13; `NSPopover` dates to macOS 10.7 and status-item behavior controls to macOS 10.12. Sources: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/menubarextra, https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/menubarextrastyle/window, https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appkit/nsstatusitem, https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appkit/nspopover.

Runtime architecture: use a `@MainActor` observable application model, an `MSWClient` actor, and a command-runner actor. Resolve and validate the executable at `~/.local/bin/msw` or a user-selected canonical path; never depend on Finder’s abbreviated PATH. Supply a deterministic environment containing Homebrew and system locations because `msw` locates `msb`, SSH, Zed, and related tools through PATH. Execute the CLI directly with Foundation `Process` and argument arrays—never concatenate shell commands. Drain stdout and stderr concurrently, cap retained output, redact credential-shaped values, attach a termination handler, and expose cancellation and explicit timeouts. Apple notes that child processes inherit an app’s sandbox and that `terminationHandler` completion is independent of `waitUntilExit`: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/process and https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/process/terminationhandler.

Serialize state-changing operations per workspace and use a global exclusion lane for all-workspace or maintenance commands. Coalesce status refreshes so only one `msw status` runs at once. Do not cancel start, stop, or restart merely because the popover closes; application-owned tasks should finish and publish results. On app quit, interrupt tracked children, allow a short grace period, then terminate them, but never implicitly stop a VM. Poll status about every 5 seconds while visible and every 30–60 seconds while hidden, refresh immediately after actions and system wake, and suspend polling during sleep. Treat parse failures as unknown rather than stopped.

Exact-CLI constraints: `msw status` currently emits a human-readable `msb ps` table followed by ports, with no stable JSON contract, so its parser must be fixture-tested and gated by `msw version`; an unrecognized version must show unsupported output rather than guess VM state. `msw start` can wait for VM ping and guest systemd for minutes, while stop delegates a 60-second timeout. Provide generous command-specific deadlines and visible progress. The dashboard may safely expose start, stop, restart, refresh, open URL, Open in Ghostty, and Open in Zed. Interactive or destructive flows—setup, GitHub token setup, push confirmation, restore, backup, resize, upgrade, volume cleanup, logs, metrics watch, and tunnels—belong in Ghostty so the CLI retains its prompts, TTY, and cancellation semantics.

Opening applications and URLs: for websites, run `msw start WORKSPACE`, then `msw url WORKSPACE PORT SCHEME`; validate the returned value as an HTTP or HTTPS URL before passing it to `NSWorkspace.open` or SwiftUI’s `openURL`. Do not reconstruct hostnames or published-port policy in the app. Apple’s URL-opening APIs follow system conventions: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appkit/nsworkspace and https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/openurlaction. To open Ghostty, locate its application URL through Launch Services and use `NSWorkspace.openApplication` with `OpenConfiguration`, `createsNewApplicationInstance = true`, and arguments `-e`, the canonical MSW path, workspace, and optional relative path. Never use AppleScript or a quoted shell string. Ghostty’s macOS CLI requires launching the graphical app and supports `-e`; its installed help was checked locally. `OpenConfiguration.arguments` is ignored for sandboxed callers, another reason this product cannot be App-Sandboxed: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appkit/nsworkspace/openconfiguration/arguments and https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appkit/nsworkspace/openapplication(at:configuration:completionhandler:). For Zed, invoke the exact `msw zed WORKSPACE [PATH]` command because it starts the VM, validates paths, and emits the supported `ssh://root@WORKSPACE.msb/workspace/...` target. Zed documents that SSH URLs use the local SSH configuration: https://zed.dev/docs/remote-development.

Administrative setup and XPC: phase one should not ship a root helper. Open the existing `setup.sh` or `msw host repair` in Ghostty and let the CLI own its administrator prompt and user-visible transaction. This preserves the current behavior, which combines root changes to loopback aliases, `/etc/hosts`, and a LaunchDaemon with per-user SSH configuration. Never run that script wholesale as root from the GUI.

If native repair is later required, split the contract first. User-owned SSH and configuration work remains unprivileged. A tiny, separately signed root daemon performs only fixed, typed operations for the three compiled loopback addresses and host records. Package its plist in `Contents/Library/LaunchDaemons`, use a bundle-relative `BundleProgram`, install the app in `/Applications`, and register it with `SMAppService.daemon(plistName:)`. `SMAppService` is available from macOS 13; approved daemons bootstrap at boot, while registration requires administrator approval in System Settings. `SMJobBless` is deprecated from macOS 13. Sources: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/servicemanagement/smappservice, https://developer.apple.com/documentation/servicemanagement/updating-helper-executables-from-earlier-versions-of-macos, and https://developer.apple.com/documentation/servicemanagement/smappservice/register().

The privileged daemon must offer no arbitrary command, path, environment, script, or file-write API. Use a versioned `NSXPCInterface` with operations such as inspect, installFixedHostRecords, and ensureFixedLoopbackAliases; validate all inputs again in the daemon, perform atomic bounded writes, return structured errors, and log without secrets. Require the app’s Team ID and bundle identifier on the daemon listener and the daemon’s identity on the client using `setConnectionCodeSigningRequirement`, available from macOS 13. Reject all other clients before exporting the interface. Apple explicitly recommends code-signing requirements for XPC peers: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/nsxpcconnection/setcodesigningrequirement(_:). Do not give the root helper Keychain access.

Login launch: use `SMAppService.mainApp.register()` and expose its `status` plus a button to open Login Items settings when approval is required. This API is available from macOS 13. Do not install a LaunchAgent merely to start the same menu app, do not use deprecated `SMLoginItemSetEnabled`, and do not auto-start the three VMs at login unless the user explicitly opts in. VM persistence is owned by MicroSandbox; the menu app observes it.

Sandbox, signing, and release: distribute directly with Developer ID and leave App Sandbox disabled. App Sandbox is mandatory for the Mac App Store but optional for Developer ID distribution; it restricts external executables, filesystem configuration, and child processes, and `NSWorkspace` ignores launch arguments for sandboxed callers. Security-scoped bookmarks cannot make arbitrary external executable workflows equivalent. Sources: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/protecting-user-data-with-app-sandbox and https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/accessing-files-from-the-macos-app-sandbox. Enable Hardened Runtime for the app and every bundled helper, retain library validation, and request no JIT, unsigned-memory, DYLD, Apple-events, or library-validation exceptions. Sign nested code inside-out with Developer ID Application, use secure timestamps, notarize with Xcode or `notarytool`, staple the ticket, and verify signatures, Gatekeeper assessment, registration, upgrade, and uninstall on clean macOS 26 systems. Apple requires Hardened Runtime for notarization: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/hardened-runtime and https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/notarizing-macos-software-before-distribution.

Keychain: the first release should never read or duplicate GitHub tokens. The existing CLI owns generic-password items under `msw.github.read` and `msw.github.write`; the app launches MSW and stores only nonsecret UI preferences. Never persist command environments or full output containing secrets. If credential management becomes native later, use Security framework `SecItem` APIs, one service/account tuple per workspace, explicit access control, and a reviewed migration because the app’s code identity and the CLI-created item ACL may differ. Keychain is intended for small encrypted secrets: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/keychain-services.

Liquid Glass and accessibility: build with the macOS 26 SDK and allow standard AppKit/SwiftUI controls and the popover to adopt the system appearance automatically. `glassEffect`, `GlassEffectContainer`, glass button styles, and AppKit `NSGlassEffectView` are macOS 26 APIs. Use custom glass only for one compact header or primary action group; do not put an independent glass surface behind each VM row. Three dense rows at roughly 380–420 points wide should use system labels, monospaced secondary metrics, restrained separators, and standard-size controls. State must be conveyed by text and symbol as well as color. Supply VoiceOver names and values, keyboard navigation, visible focus, sufficient contrast, and test Reduce Transparency, Increase Contrast, Differentiate Without Color, and Reduce Motion. Disable custom morphing and replace custom translucent surfaces with an opaque system background when requested. Apple advises using standard components, testing accessibility settings, and avoiding overuse: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technologyoverviews/adopting-liquid-glass and https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/glasseffect(_:in:). If supporting macOS 13–15 later, guard custom glass with `if #available(macOS 26, *)` and use system material or plain backgrounds as fallback.

Phases: (0) freeze a versioned MSW command/output contract and fixtures for 3.1.0. (1) ship the AppKit status item, SwiftUI three-row popover, asynchronous command runner, lifecycle actions, URL opening, and Ghostty/Zed handoffs—without a helper. (2) add login launch, settings, wake-aware polling, accessibility audits, cancellation, and failure recovery. (3) only after separating root and user setup responsibilities, add the narrowly scoped SMAppService/XPC daemon and migration/uninstall flow. (4) archive, sign, notarize, staple, and run clean-machine release tests covering missing CLI/config/apps, denied Login Items or daemon approval, sleeping during operations, malformed status output, concurrent actions, upgrade, and removal.

Verification: inspected the current README, setup guide, command cheatsheet, and relevant MSW 3.1.0 command paths; checked API availability against the installed Xcode 26.5 macOS SDK and current Apple documentation; checked Ghostty and Zed installed CLI help; and confirmed the worktree after inspection. No files were edited and no tests, formatters, or linters were run. Pre-existing worktree changes were left untouched.","filesChanged":[]}
